accost

/uh-KOST/ - rhymes with frost · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Accost means to approach and confront someone aggressively.

A man with a clipboard accosted me in the parking lot, planting himself between my cart and the car until I heard his pitch.

Example

Halfway up the library steps, the city treasurer was accosted by a stranger who seized her elbow and demanded to know why the fountain was dry; she kept a guard with her after that.

Accost is more than approach and sharper than greet: it names an approach that corners someone — sudden, unwelcome, and edged with aggression. You approach a teacher after class; you accost someone when you cut off their path and force the encounter.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

waylay: To waylay someone is to stop them mid-route, often by lying in wait along the path they must take. It can even be friendly — a colleague can waylay you by the elevator with good news. Accost is never friendly: the approach itself is aggressive, unwelcome, and forced on its target.

buttonhole: To buttonhole someone is to corner them into a conversation they did not ask for — pushy, but not menacing. Accost is harsher: it carries real aggression, an edge of threat. A chatty neighbor buttonholes you about the fence; a stranger who blocks your path and makes demands accosts you.

ambush: To ambush someone is to spring on them from concealment — the surprise is the whole point, and the ambusher hides until the last second. Accost needs no hiding place: the aggressor simply walks up in the open and forces the encounter. Reporters ambush an official from behind a doorway; they accost him face-on in the street.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

avoid: steer clear of someone entirely

shun: deliberately keep away from a person, pointedly

Where it sits · how forceful and unwelcome the encounter is — approach → confront → accost

approach vs. accost: Anyone can approach you politely to ask the time; approach carries none of the heat that accost promises.

confront vs. accost: Confront means facing someone directly, even quietly and fairly — it stops short of accost, which rushes an unwilling stranger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ac-

Prefix — ac-: to, toward (a form of ad-)

Root — cost

Root — cost: rib, side (Latin costa)

Put it together

Put it together: Ac- (toward) + cost (side) = to come up to someone's side. French sailors used accoster for laying a ship alongside another; on land it became pulling up alongside a person — and English narrowed it to the uninvited, menacing kind of pulling up.

Use the root in a new word: coast

Use the root in a new word: coast: The highway hugs the coast — the land's side, its rib against the sea — for eighty miles.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / journalistic

Accost is the reporter's word for an aggressive, unwelcome approach — stronger than stop or approach, less physical than attack. If the encounter escalates into a storm of words or blows, you have moved past accost into assail territory (also in this unit).
